卡林巴以拇指或手指撥動金屬彈片發聲，泛音不諧和，起音時最強，隨後迅速衰減，留下接: The kalimba sounds when the metal tines are plucked with the thumbs or fingers; the overtones are inharmonic, strongest at the attack and then dying away quickly to leave something close to a pure tone; neighbouring tines vibrate a second time and complicate a single note. The lowest note is in the centre and the higher ones on either side, and the seven-note sequence can exceed a Western octave, its intervals unlike equal temperament. Unlike strings or wind, the timbre comes from the vibrating tine, not a string or an air column. The source does not fully cover how volume is controlled.
卡林巴（Kalimba，又稱姆比拉 Mbira），源自辛巴威紹納人的體鳴樂器，H: The kalimba (also called mbira), an idiophone from the Shona people of Zimbabwe, H-S 122.1. It is built as a wooden board, often with a resonator, carrying staggered metal tines; the player holds it in both hands and plucks the tines with the thumbs or fingers. It belongs to the lamellophone family among plucked idiophones. In eastern and southern Africa such instruments often play with percussion such as the hosho, for religious ritual, weddings and social gatherings.
卡林巴／姆比拉常見於辛巴威紹納人的宗教儀式、婚禮與社交聚會，東南部非洲也常以 霍: The kalimba / mbira is common in the religious ritual, weddings and social gatherings of the Shona of Zimbabwe, and in south-eastern Africa it is often accompanied by the percussion of the hosho drum. On the modern stage Maurice White and Thomas Mapfumo have brought the mbira into a modern rock line-up of electric guitar, bass, jazz drums and brass, drawing on traditional pieces; for example mbira dzavadzimu pieces such as Kariga mombe. Dumisani Maraire also brought marimba and kalimba music to the Pacific Northwest of the United States, and Ephat Mujuru taught mbira dzavadzimu in the United States.
卡林巴／姆比拉的琴身通常為木製琴板，板上裝有錯落排列的金屬彈片，演奏者以拇指或手: The body of the kalimba / mbira is usually a wooden board carrying staggered metal tines, which the player plucks with the thumbs or fingers. The tines were once made of bamboo and later of metal; some boards also have a resonator, but the material of the resonator and other fittings is not recorded.

演奏時以雙手托住琴身，使金屬彈片朝上，再以拇指或手指撥動彈片發聲。初學可先固定持: To play, cradle the body in both hands with the metal tines facing up, then pluck the tines with the thumbs or fingers. Beginners can fix the holding position first and practise the thumb stroke one tine at a time, then bring in the index finger, watching the spacing of the tines and the layout of the pitches. On a traditional kalimba the lower notes are often in the centre and the higher ones to either side, so the thumbs can turn to reach different tines.

非洲撥奏體鳴樂器已有數千年歷史。約三千年前，西非出現木或竹彈片樂器；約一千三百年: Plucked idiophones have been made in Africa for thousands of years. About three thousand years ago wooden or bamboo tine instruments appeared in West Africa; about thirteen hundred years ago metal-tine instruments appeared in the Zambezi valley and then spread across Africa, developing different forms and social uses among the Shona of Zimbabwe and in Mozambique. In the mid-twentieth century the ethnomusicologist Hugh Tracey designed the kalimba on the model of the mbira nyunga nyunga, and it was commercially exported from the late 1950s, which made it popular outside Africa. In 2020 the making and playing of the mbira/sansi in Malawi and Zimbabwe was inscribed on the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage.
